title: Blessed in Christ, Before the World Began
sum: The letter opens with one very long sentence of praise (1:3-14, 202 words in Greek) that tells the whole story of God's plan. The Father chose a people in Christ before the world began and decided beforehand to adopt them. The Son redeemed them by his blood and forgave their trespasses. The Spirit is the seal and down payment of the inheritance still to come. At the center stands God's purpose, kept secret until now, to bring all things in heaven and on earth together in Christ (1:9-10).

Paul then reports his prayer for the readers (1:15-23). He has heard of their faith and love and asks God to give them wisdom to know him, to see the hope of their calling, the wealth of his inheritance and the greatness of the power that works for them. That power raised Christ from the dead and seated him above every ruler and authority, and made him head of the church, which is his body. The chapter is praise first, then prayer, and it tells the readers who they are before it tells them what to do.
readings: Read as a hymn of the Trinity

Many readers hear a three-part praise: the Father who chose and decided (1:3-6), the Son who redeemed and gathered (1:7-12), and the Spirit who seals (1:13-14). Each part ends on 'to the praise of his glory' (1:6, 12, 14). Ancient and modern preachers have used this structure to teach the Trinity, though Paul does not present it as a doctrine.
Read as a story of Israel and the nations

Others hear the 'we' of 1:3-12 as Jewish believers and the 'you' of 1:13 as Gentiles, so that the passage tells how God's choice of Israel (election, adoption, inheritance, redemption) has now opened to the nations through the Messiah. The 'we' and 'you' then lead straight into the unity of chapter 2.
Read as a letter-opening in the style of a Jewish prayer
The blessing 'Blessed be God' follows the form of Jewish thanksgiving prayers. On this reading the passage is first of all worship, and its teaching comes through praise and not through argument.

views.H: Ephesus was the leading city of the Roman province of Asia, with its great temple of Artemis, a large Jewish community (Acts 19:8-10), and a strong tradition of magic (Acts 19:19). The letter is addressed to Gentile believers (2:11; 3:1) living among powers they once served. To them, words such as 'chosen', 'adopted', 'redeemed' and 'sealed' had everyday meanings: citizens were enrolled, children were adopted into Roman families, slaves were bought and set free, and documents and goods were sealed. The claim that Christ sits 'far above every ruler and authority' (1:21) was heard in a world of emperor worship and local gods. The date and the place from which Paul wrote (Rome, Caesarea or Ephesus) are discussed at 3:1.
views.C: Three critical questions meet in chapter 1. First, whether 'in Ephesus' belongs in 1:1 (the variant). Second, authorship: the 202-word sentence of 1:3-14 and the 169-word sentence of 1:15-23 have no match in Paul's undisputed letters, and Colossians 1 has close echoes of 1:7, 1:9-10 and 1:20-23. Lincoln, Best and Schnackenburg take this as evidence of a follower of Paul; defenders of Paul reply that Paul wrote a different style when he prayed, and that a letter carrier or secretary helps explain the differences. Third, 1:15 ('since I heard of your faith') seems odd from the man who lived among them for three years (Acts 19:8-10; 20:31). The book page gives the full discussion.
views.L: The long sentence is held together by repeating phrases: 'in him', 'in Christ', 'in the Beloved' appear about a dozen times, with 'to the praise of his glory' three times, and strings of 'according to' and 'which'. The Plain breaks it into short sentences but keeps the order of the Greek. The words come in pairs and triples (wisdom and understanding, will and good pleasure and purpose, power and might and strength) that give the style of a prayer rather than an argument. The prayer of 1:15-23 is another single Greek sentence, and it ends with a series of statements about Christ's rule that run on from Psalm 110:1 and Psalm 8:6.
views.J: The chapter is full of Israel's vocabulary: chosen (Deuteronomy 7:6-7), holy and blameless, adoption (Israel is God's firstborn son, Exodus 4:22), redemption (the Exodus), inheritance (Israel as the LORD's share, Deuteronomy 32:9), the seal and the people God has made his own (Exodus 19:5). Jewish readers will notice that the benefits of Israel are now given to Gentiles, and also that Paul does not say Israel's election is canceled; he says these gifts reach the nations through the Messiah. Jewish thought also knew of things planned before the world was made (the Torah, the name of the Messiah; Pesahim 54a) and of the 'two ages' of 1:21. A Jewish reader may ask whether 'in Christ' replaces being in the covenant or widens it; the churches' answers are on the cards at 3:6.
views.T: The chapter has been central to church teaching on election and predestination: Augustine, Aquinas, Calvin and Wesley all wrote on it, and the card shows the main answers. Chrysostom's 24 homilies on Ephesians take the long sentence in turn; in Homily 2 he says Paul takes every chance to show God's great loving-kindness toward us. Irenaeus built his doctrine of 'recapitulation' on 1:10. On 1:13-14, Catholic and Orthodox teaching ties the seal to baptism and chrismation or confirmation, and the Reformed and Baptist traditions to the moment of faith; see the card. On 1:22-23, all traditions teach that the church is Christ's body, but they disagree about how visible and how united it must be; see the card on the book page.

deep.h: One sentence in Greek: how 1:3-14 is built
deep.b:
In the Greek, verses 3 to 14 are one unbroken sentence. There is no full stop, only a chain of phrases hooked together with 'who', 'in whom', 'according to', 'for' and 'to'. Translators must cut it up, and where they cut changes where the reader's eye falls. The Plain cuts at the main steps: the blessing (1:3), the choice and adoption (1:4-6), the redemption and the secret (1:7-10), the inheritance (1:11-12) and the seal (1:13-14).

Several things hold it together. The little phrase en Christo ('in Christ', 'in him') returns about a dozen times, so that everything God does, he does in Christ. The refrain 'to the praise of his glory' marks off three movements. And the verbs of God's activity pile up: blessed, chose, decided beforehand, freely gave, made overflow, made known, purposed, works. The single subject is God. The readers, 'we' and 'you', are all object of the verbs, and the only thing they do is hear, believe and hope (1:12-13).

This is the usual Jewish and early Christian way of blessing God: to say what he has done, and to do it without drawing breath. Whether the passage was an earlier hymn that Paul or a follower took over, or was composed for the letter, is disputed.

deep.h: Chosen in Christ: the Old Testament background of election
deep.b:
The verb 'chose' (eklegomai) comes from the Greek Old Testament, where God chooses Israel from all the nations: 'The LORD your God has chosen you out of all the peoples on the face of the ground to be his people' (Deuteronomy 7:6). The choice was not because Israel was great (Deuteronomy 7:7-8) and it had a purpose: to be holy, a people set apart for him. Paul keeps those two points: the choice is God's initiative ('before the foundation of the world') and the purpose is holiness ('to be holy and without blame'). He changes one thing: the choice is 'in Christ'.

That small phrase is where the disagreements start. If Christ is the chosen one (Isaiah 42:1), then those 'in him' share his election, and the question 'who is in him?' becomes the question of election. The card shows how the traditions answer. One point is not in dispute: Paul uses election as a ground for praise, not as a puzzle to be solved. In Ephesians nobody is told who is not chosen.

deep.title: Spec: the blessing as a map of the whole letter
deep.b:
Claude's theory, not an established reading. The three movements of 1:3-14 may be a table of contents for the letter. The Father's choice and adoption (1:4-6) are answered in chapter 2 by the readers' own story (dead, then made alive by grace, 2:1-10) and in chapter 3 by 'every family... gets its name from him' (3:14-15). The Son's redemption and the gathering of all things (1:7-10) are answered by the one new humanity (2:11-22) and the plan of the mystery (3:1-13). The Spirit's seal and down payment (1:13-14) are answered by 'access in one Spirit' (2:18), 'a home for God in the Spirit' (2:22) and the prayer for strength through the Spirit (3:16), and by 4:30 ('do not make the Holy Spirit sad, who sealed you'). If this holds, 1:3-14 is both an opening prayer and an outline of the letter.

I have not seen the precise mapping of the three movements onto the three following chapters in print.

echoes: Deuteronomy 7:6-8; Exodus 4:22; Exodus 19:5; Deuteronomy 32:9; Psalm 110:1; Psalm 8:6; Isaiah 42:1; Romans 8:28-30; Romans 8:15-23; 2 Corinthians 1:3; 2 Corinthians 1:21-22; Galatians 4:4-7; Colossians 1:9-23; 1 Peter 1:3-5; 1 Peter 1:20

settings.by: Paul, as the letter names him
settings.to: the saints 'in Ephesus' (some of the oldest manuscripts leave out the city), faithful in Christ Jesus: Gentile believers, with Jewish believers among them, in the province of Asia
settings.when: while Paul is in prison (3:1; 4:1; 6:20); Rome (about AD 62 on the traditional dating) is the commonest view, Caesarea or Ephesus are also proposed, and some scholars hold that a follower of Paul wrote the letter after his death
settings.why: to name the sender with his authority as an apostle 'by the will of God', and to give the usual blessing of grace and peace. The words 'in Ephesus' decide who the first readers were: one church, or a group of churches. The two blanks in our knowledge, the author's situation and the readers' city, change how the whole letter is heard.
settings.readers: A Gentile Christian in Asia, hearing a letter from the apostle to the Gentiles read aloud at a meeting, would hear his own community called 'saints', a title that had belonged to Israel.
views: The words are original or at least the address of the copy kept at Ephesus; the letter was for the church there and for others near it, with a general tone because it was meant to be shared (held by many).
The blank was filled by each church that received a copy (a view held by many); 'in Ephesus' was added when the collection of Paul's letters was made there.
A letter from a later disciple
The writer addressed Christians of Asia in general, in Paul's name, perhaps with Colossians 4:16 ('the letter from Laodicea') as his starting point.

settings.to: the Gentile believers of the letter's address, with Jewish believers included in 'we' (1:3-12) and Gentile believers in 'you also' (1:13)
settings.when: as the opening of the letter, before any teaching or instruction
settings.why: to place the readers inside a story far older than themselves. Gentile believers, who had belonged to no covenant (2:12), are told that they were chosen before the world began, adopted, redeemed and sealed. The praise comes first because the readers need to know what has been given before they are asked to live it; and it prepares for the argument of chapter 2 that Jews and Gentiles share it.
settings.readers: For readers who may have felt like latecomers in a movement that began among Jews in Jerusalem, 'before the foundation of the world' reached back past Moses and Abraham.
views: Some scholars hold that Paul or a later writer built on an earlier Christian hymn of praise. The repeated 'in him' and the rhythm of the clauses are the main evidence.
Others hold that the passage is the natural flow of a man who prayed and wrote in long sentences, with no need for an earlier hymn.

settings.to: the readers, as 'I do not stop giving thanks for you'
settings.when: after Paul 'heard' of their faith and love, and during his time of imprisonment
settings.why: to tell the readers what he prays for them, which is also what he wants them to want: not new gifts but knowledge, so that they will see the hope, the inheritance and the power that is theirs. The point is that they know already (1:3-14) but do not yet see, and the prayer asks for eyes. Prayer reports like this one teach by showing the readers what to pray.
settings.readers: Believers living among powers they had once feared would hear that the power at work for them is the same that raised Christ and set him above every power.
views: The prayer reports in Paul's letters (Philippians 1:9-11; Colossians 1:9-14; Ephesians 3:14-19) are commonly read as teaching in the form of prayer, saying to the readers what Paul wants for them, so that they learn it as they listen.

traditions.q: Does 'he chose us in Christ' mean God chose particular persons for salvation?
views: Predestination is real: God marks out those who will be saved, and the saints' glory is his gift (Aquinas, Summa Theologiae I, q. 23). But God predestines no one to hell; damnation needs a person's own turning away (Catechism 1037).

Chrysostom, in his first homily on Ephesians, reads 'chose us' and 'predestined us' this way: predestination 'comes not of any pains, nor of any good works of ours, but of love; and yet not of love alone, but of our virtue also.' He says election 'is the result neither of His love alone, nor yet of our virtue, but of both.' He also says God 'has Himself rendered us holy, but then we must continue holy.'

Election is 'in Christ' and is known only through Christ and the gospel, never by searching God's hidden counsel (Solid Declaration XI). The Formula of Concord teaches that God's election not only foresees the salvation of the elect but is also a cause which procures, works, helps and promotes their salvation, and that nothing in us is a cause of God's election (Solid Declaration XI 8, 88). It is taught so that troubled Christians can take comfort from it.

God chose particular persons before the foundation of the world, not on foreseen faith but by his own will, and Christ is the one in whom they are chosen (Westminster Confession 3.5; Canons of Dort I; Calvin, Institutes 3.21-24). Karl Barth, in the Reformed line, rejected the idea of a hidden decree and made Jesus Christ himself the object of election, with humanity's election found in him.

Article 17 teaches that predestination to life is God's eternal purpose, that those chosen are chosen 'in Christ', and that thinking on it is a comfort to the godly but a danger to 'curious and carnal persons'.

Wesley taught that God chose in Christ those whom he foreknew would believe: election is conditional, grace is free to all, and God's preventing grace makes a response possible. He rejected unconditional election as contrary to God's justice and love for all (Free Grace; Sermon 43, The Scripture Way of Salvation).

Baptists are divided. The 1689 London Confession (chapter 3) follows the Westminster Confession in speaking of God's decree. The Baptist Faith and Message (2000, article 5) calls election 'the gracious purpose of God' and says it is consistent with the free agency of man.

traditions.q: When are believers 'sealed with the Holy Spirit' (1:13)?
views: The seal is the spiritual mark given in baptism and confirmation; the Catechism speaks of the 'seal of the Holy Spirit' as the sign of belonging to Christ for ever (Catechism 1295-1296).
The seal is given in chrismation, the anointing with holy oil that the Eastern churches ordinarily give immediately after baptism; its formula speaks of the seal of the gift of the Holy Spirit.

Lutherans tie the Spirit's work to the gospel and to baptism: in the Small Catechism the Holy Spirit 'has called me by the Gospel', and Baptism 'works forgiveness of sins, delivers from death and the devil, and gives eternal salvation to all who believe'.

The sealing is the Spirit's inward assurance, given in the believer's faith and growing in it (Westminster Confession 18.2, which cites this verse). Baptism is a sign and seal of the covenant of grace (Westminster Confession 28.1).
The Baptist Faith and Message (2000, article 2) says the Holy Spirit 'seals the believer unto the day of final redemption.' It does not tie the sealing to a rite such as baptism or confirmation.

Many Pentecostals teach a baptism in the Holy Spirit as a separate experience after conversion, usually shown by speaking in tongues, and read 1:13 together with Acts 19:2 ("When you came to believe, did you receive the Holy Spirit?").

title: Dead, Made Alive, and One New Humanity
sum: The chapter has two halves. In 2:1-10 Paul reminds the readers what they were and what God did. They were dead in their trespasses, following the age of this world and its unseen ruler, and under God's anger like everyone else. But God, rich in mercy, made them alive together with Christ, raised them and seated them in the heavenly world. They are saved by grace, through faith, as a gift and not a reward for works, and they were made to do good works that God prepared for them.

In 2:11-22 the story turns from the individual to the community. Gentiles were once outsiders to Israel's citizenship and covenants. Now, by Christ's blood, they have been brought near. Christ himself is the peace between two peoples: he broke down the dividing wall, ended the hostility and created in himself one new humanity out of the two. Together they have access to the Father in one Spirit and are being built into a household, a building and a holy temple. The chapter answers two questions at once: how can a person be put right with God, and how can two enemy peoples live as one?
readings: Read as the story of one person, then of a people
The first half is about being rescued from death; the second is about being brought into a community. Many readers see them as two sides of one rescue: you cannot be saved alone.
Read as a map of the Temple

2:11-22 moves from the outer court (the Gentiles 'far off'), through the barrier, to the nearness of 'access', to the inner house where God lives. On this reading the whole passage is a pilgrim's walk into the sanctuary, which the church has become.
Read as the answer to a quarrel

If Jewish and Gentile believers in Asia were suspicious of each other, the passage works as a peace treaty: the Gentiles are reminded of their former exclusion (so they do not boast, compare Romans 11:17-24), and the Jews are told that the wall they valued has been taken down by the Messiah himself.

views.H: Ephesus in the 50s and 60s: a city of Artemis worship, magic and the emperor's cult, with a Jewish community (Acts 19:8-10). Gentiles who joined the synagogue as 'God-fearers' were welcome to listen but not to share in all of Jewish life, and in Jerusalem a notice in the Temple threatened any foreigner with death if he went beyond the barrier (Josephus, Jewish War 5.193-194). Paul himself was arrested in Jerusalem on a charge of bringing Trophimus, an Ephesian, past it (Acts 21:27-29). The 'wall' was no distant idea to the readers of Ephesus.
views.C: Four points. (1) 2:5-6: believers have already been raised and seated with Christ, where Romans 6 puts the raising in the future; some take this as a mark of a later writer, defenders of Paul as Paul's own 'already and not yet'. (2) 2:15: 'put out of effect the law of commandments with its rules' is unlike Romans 7:12, which calls the law holy, and some find a later and more negative view of the law, while others note that Paul can say both things in different settings. (3) 2:20: the apostles and prophets as a past foundation. (4) Close echoes of Colossians 1:21-22 and 2:11-15, and the variants at 2:15 and 2:17 (KJV 'in himself'; one 'peace' instead of two).
views.L: Two panels, each with the pattern 'once... but now'. In 2:1-10 the verbs move from 'you were dead... walked... lived' to 'But God... made us alive together, raised us up together, seated us together'. In 2:11-22 the pattern is 'once you were... but now in Christ Jesus you have come near'. The first half uses 'you' and 'we' by turns (the Gentile readers, then Paul and his fellow Jews with them in the same condition); the second is 'you' and 'both'. The chapter piles up images for the church: a body (2:16), a polis with citizens (2:19), a household (2:19), a building on a foundation (2:20) and a temple (2:21-22). The prefix 'with' (syn) runs through it (made alive with, raised with, seated with, citizens with, fitted together, built together).
views.J: Paul writes as a Jew to Gentiles about a Jewish privilege that has been opened. 'Commonwealth of Israel', 'the covenants of the promise' and 'hope' are Israel's things. The Gentile readers are not told that they have replaced Israel, and not told that Israel has been set aside; they are told that they have been brought near to what already exists. The prophets had looked for this (Isaiah 2:2-4; 56:3-8; 57:19). The troubling sentence for Jewish readers is 2:15 ('the law of commandments... put out of effect'); in the Christian past it was often read as saying the Law of Moses was ended for the Jews too, and it fed contempt for Jewish practice. Some scholars read the sentence as about how Gentiles are admitted, not about what Jews must give up. The question is open and the card sets out the churches' positions.
views.T: 2:8-10 became one of the great texts of the Reformation: cited for salvation by grace alone through faith alone, and it is just as central to Catholic teaching on grace at Trent. Augustine used 2:3 for original sin (On Marriage and Concupiscence, book 2) and quoted 2:8-10 in On the Spirit and the Letter while asking where faith itself comes from. Wesley's sermon 'The Scripture Way of Salvation' is an exposition of 2:8. Chrysostom preached through the whole letter in a series of 24 homilies. 2:20 is cited in support of apostolic succession (Catholic, Orthodox, Anglican) and for Scripture alone (Lutheran, Reformed, Baptist); see the card.

deep.h: By grace through faith: the verse and the argument
deep.b:
Verses 8-9 are the most quoted lines of Ephesians. Their wording is simple: you have been saved; the means is grace, not works; faith is the way it is received; and none of it comes from yourselves. Two points keep the verse from being misread. First, it sits inside a longer movement (2:1-10) that goes from death to life to good works. The 'not from works' of verse 9 is balanced by 'created in Christ Jesus to do good works' in verse 10, so 'works' are the purpose of salvation, not the price of it. Second, 'works' here is the opposite of 'grace', not the opposite of 'faith'; Paul is not setting an active life against a passive one.

The churches agree on the first half and divide on the rest. Catholics hold that grace is an unearned gift that works in the person and brings forth merit that is itself God's gift (Trent session 6; Catechism 2008-2011). Lutherans and Reformed teach that a person is declared right with God by faith alone, and that works are the fruit and sign of faith, not part of its ground. Methodists add that faith is itself made possible by prevenient grace and that holiness is the goal. Orthodox teachers prefer to speak of salvation as healing and union with God in which grace and human effort work together. The note at 2:8 on the neuter 'this' and the card below give the detail. James 2:14-26 uses 'justify' and 'works' of the proof of a living faith before others, which is a different question; compare the note at 2:9.

deep.h: The wall, the law and the new humanity
deep.b:
Verses 14-16 are packed. Christ 'made the two one', 'broke down the middle wall', 'ended the hostility', 'put the law of commandments out of effect', 'created in him one new humanity', 'reconciled both in one body through the cross', and 'killed the hostility'. Three of these concern a barrier (the wall, the law, the hostility), and three concern a union (one, new humanity, one body).

The wall had several faces. There was the Temple's stone barrier with its warning notices in Greek and Latin. There was the law as a fence, as in the Letter of Aristeas, which describes Moses fencing Israel about with palisades and iron walls of law to prevent mixing with other peoples. And there was the hostility itself, the mutual contempt between Jews and Gentiles in every city of the empire. Paul does not need to choose between them: all three are removed in Christ. What he says is put out of effect is 'the law of commandments in decrees', a phrase that has been read as the whole law, its ceremonial part, its function as a barrier, its curse or its condemnation (see the note at 2:15 and the card). He does not say the law was wrong. In Romans 7:12 he calls it holy, and in Galatians 3:24-25 it was a guardian until Christ came.

The result is a new thing: neither Jews who become Gentiles nor Gentiles who become Jews, but a third body, 'one new humanity', that includes both without erasing either. How far that leaves room for Jews to keep practicing their ancestral law is argued today by Christian and Jewish scholars; the earliest churches struggled with it (Acts 15; Galatians 2).

deep.title: Spec: 2:11-22 as a walk through the Temple
deep.b:
Claude's theory, not an established reading. The movement of 2:13-22 follows a path through the Jerusalem Temple in reverse of the way Gentiles were kept out. 'Far away' is outside the Temple Mount's barrier (2:13). The dividing wall is the barrier with its warning notices (2:14). 'Access' is passing the barrier and entering the court (2:18; the related Greek verb prosago is used of bringing offerings near God). 'Citizens... household' is membership of the community that worships there (2:19). The 'foundation', 'cornerstone', 'building' and 'a temple that is holy in the Lord' (2:20-21) are the sanctuary itself, and the last step is the 'home for God in the Spirit' (2:22), the Holy of Holies where God dwelt. A Gentile reader who had heard of Jerusalem's Temple, and an Ephesian who knew the great temple of Artemis in his own city, would hear the same journey: from the street to the place of the god, with no barrier left.

This overlaps with scholars who see Temple imagery in 2:14-22 and with the older view that the wall is the Temple barrier. I have not seen the passage read as a full pilgrim's path in print.

echoes: Genesis 17:9-14; Isaiah 2:2-4; Isaiah 28:16; Isaiah 56:3-8; Isaiah 57:19; Isaiah 52:7; Psalm 118:22; Exodus 25:8; Ezekiel 44:6-9; Romans 3:21-31; Romans 5:1-2; Romans 6:1-14; Romans 11:17-24; Galatians 2:11-21; Galatians 3:26-29; Colossians 1:21-22; Colossians 2:11-15; Acts 15:1-29; Acts 21:27-36; 1 Corinthians 3:9-17; 1 Peter 2:4-10

settings.what: Dead, made alive, saved by grace
settings.to: the Gentile readers ('you', 2:1-2), then Paul and fellow Jewish believers together with them ('we', 2:3-10)
settings.when: within the praise and prayer of the letter's first half, before the call to unity
settings.why: to remind the readers of their rescue and to close off any boast about it. The Gentile readers learn that their old life belonged to the powers of this age. The Jewish readers learn that 'we all' were in the same condition (2:3). Both are told that salvation is a gift, so that neither can claim the better place. The final turn to 'good works' (2:10) prepares for the call to live differently in chapters 4 to 6.
settings.readers: In a city of magic and many gods, believers would hear that the 'ruler of the domain of the air' and the spirit now at work in the disobedient are the powers they once served, and that these no longer have the last word.
views: 'We all' may be Jewish believers added to the Gentile 'you' (so that all are under sin, as in Romans 3:9-23), or the whole Christian group in the letter's voice. In either case Paul includes himself.

settings.to: the Gentile readers ('you Gentiles in the flesh', 2:11), with Jewish believers included as the 'both' of 2:14-18
settings.when: as the second half of the first great teaching of the letter, after the personal rescue of 2:1-10
settings.why: to say what the rescue means for a community: the dividing line between Jew and Gentile has been taken away, so the Gentiles are not guests but fellow citizens and a part of God's own house. It is also a call to remember (2:11), so that the readers neither forget what they were nor look down on Jews. Without this, the unity of chapter 4 would have nothing under it.
settings.readers: In cities where Jews and Gentiles lived side by side but apart, and where Gentile believers might feel they were joining someone else's movement, the passage told them they were at home, and told Jewish believers that the barrier they valued had been removed.
views: Some scholars hear a warning to Gentile Christians not to despise Jewish believers (as in Romans 11:17-24); others find the letter calm, with no sign of any local quarrel, and read the passage as a general statement of the new situation.
Almost all scholars take the 'you' as Gentiles; a few hold that Jewish believers are addressed here as well. Nobody doubts that Jews are part of the 'both'.

traditions.q: How do grace, faith and works relate in being saved (2:8-10)?
views: Grace is a free and undeserved gift, and faith is a gift too (Catechism 153, 1996). Justification is more than forgiveness: it is a real renewing of the person by grace, and the works that follow merit eternal life only because they come from grace (Council of Trent, session 6; Catechism 2008-2011).
Salvation is God's gift, not earned; the Orthodox speak of salvation as a working together (synergeia) in which the human will accepts and cooperates with God.

A person is justified by grace through faith alone, apart from works (Augsburg Confession IV). Faith itself is the Spirit's work through the word, and good works follow as its fruit; works are not any part of the ground of justification (Formula of Concord, Solid Declaration III and IV).

Faith is the instrument by which Christ is received, and it is the gift and work of the Spirit (Westminster Confession 11 and 14.1; Heidelberg Catechism 20-21, 60-64). Good works are the fruit and evidence of true faith, never its cause.

We are accounted righteous before God only for the merit of Christ, by faith, and not for our own works (Thirty-Nine Articles, Article 11); good works follow justification and are pleasing to God in Christ (Article 12).

Wesley preached on Ephesians 2:8 in 'The Scripture Way of Salvation': salvation is by grace, in the beginning (preventing grace) and by faith, which is the condition of being justified and not a work; he spoke of waiting for entire sanctification.

Salvation is wholly of grace, received by repentance and faith in the Lord Jesus Christ, with good works as its evidence (Baptist Faith and Message 2000, article 4; London Confession 1689, chapters 11 and 14).

traditions.q: What did Christ put out of effect in 'the law of commandments with its rules' (2:15)?
views: The Old Law was a preparation for the Gospel. Its moral precepts, summed up in the Ten Commandments, remain binding; its ceremonial and judicial precepts are fulfilled in Christ and no longer bind (Aquinas, Summa Theologiae I-II, qq. 98-108; Catechism 1961-1964).

Chrysostom, in his fifth homily on Ephesians, reads 'the law of commandments' as taken away by Christ: 'He gave us a law that we should keep it, and when we kept it not, and ought to have been punished, He even abrogated the law itself.' He says the 'enmity' that Christ ended was a barrier between God and both Jews and Gentiles, not only a wall between Jew and Gentile.

The law accuses, and in that use Christ has ended its condemnation for those in him; the law remains as a guide for the world and as a mirror of sin. The distinction between law and gospel is the heart of the Lutheran reading (Formula of Concord V and VI).

The ceremonial law was abolished at Christ's coming, the judicial law expired with Israel as a state, and the moral law binds all people for ever (Westminster Confession 19). Calvin read the verse of the ceremonies that divided Jew from Gentile.

Article 7 says the law given by Moses, 'as touching Ceremonies and Rites, do not bind Christian men,' nor must its civil precepts be received in any commonwealth, but 'no Christian man whatsoever is free from the obedience of the Commandments which are called Moral.'

The Methodist Articles of Religion (1784, article VI) repeat the Anglican wording: the law given by Moses, 'as touching ceremonies and rites, doth not bind Christians,' yet no Christian is free from the moral commandments.

The 1689 London Confession (19.3) says the ceremonial laws, 'appointed only to the time of reformation,' were 'abrogated and taken away' by Jesus Christ, and cites Ephesians 2:14-16 for this. The judicial laws expired with Israel as a state, and the moral law binds all people for ever (19.4-5).

The Ten Commandments, including the seventh-day Sabbath, remain binding on all (Fundamental Belief 19). What ended at the cross were the ceremonial and sacrificial laws, which pointed to Christ's work.

Dispensationalists hold that Christ abolished the Mosaic law, so that it does not apply to the Christian, and that Israel and the church keep distinct roles; they also speak of the church as a separate program, a 'mystery'.
Messianic Jews generally consider the written Torah to remain in force, to be observed morally and ritually, revised through the apostolic writings.

traditions.q: Are there still apostles and prophets? What is the 'foundation' (2:20)?
views: The apostles are the foundation, and their office continues in the bishops, who are their successors (Lumen Gentium 20; Catechism 861). But public revelation ended with the apostles, and no new public revelation is expected before Christ's return (Catechism 66-67; Dei Verbum 4).

In the Orthodox Church there is one Tradition, which includes the scriptures and the teaching of the Church Fathers; apostolic succession is seen as a God-ordained way in which the church's structure and teaching are passed on.

The sole rule and standard by which all teaching is judged is 'the prophetic and apostolic Scriptures of the Old and of the New Testament alone' (Formula of Concord, Epitome, Rule and Norm 1). The apostles' office is not continued; their teaching is held in Scripture.

The foundation was laid once by the apostles and prophets, and the 'former ways of God's revealing his will' have ceased (Westminster Confession 1.1); Scripture is sufficient (1.6). Ministers are called to preach and teach, not to be apostles.
Scripture contains all things necessary for salvation (Article 6), and the historic episcopate is one of the four points of the Lambeth Quadrilateral (1888).

The apostles and prophets laid the foundation in the New Testament; Scripture alone is the final authority (Baptist Faith and Message 2000, article 1), and churches are governed by Christ through their own congregations, not by apostolic succession.

Pentecostals are generally continuationists about spiritual gifts. The New Apostolic Reformation, a movement tied to C. Peter Wagner, has leaders who call themselves apostles and prophets, and many Pentecostals and charismatics are concerned about its promotion of those offices (4:11).

title: The Secret Made Known, and a Prayer for Love
sum: Paul begins a sentence about himself as the prisoner of Christ Jesus for the Gentiles, then stops and explains his task (3:1-13). God gave him the job of managing his grace for them, and made known to him by revelation a secret hidden for ages: that the Gentiles are heirs together with Israel, members of one body and sharers in the promise in Christ Jesus through the good news. Paul describes himself as less than the least of the saints, given the grace to announce the riches of Christ. The purpose is that the church would show God's many-sided wisdom to the rulers and authorities in the heavenly world.

Then he picks up the broken sentence and prays (3:14-21). He kneels before the Father, from whom every family takes its name, and asks that the readers be strengthened by the Spirit, that Christ settle in their hearts, that they be rooted in love, and that with all the saints they grasp the width, length, height and depth of Christ's love and be filled with all the fullness of God. A doxology to the God who can do far beyond what we ask closes the first half of the letter.
readings: Read as the center of the letter

The 'mystery' is what the first three chapters have been moving toward: that Jews and Gentiles are one people. On this reading chapter 3 states the point of chapters 1 and 2 and prepares for the call to unity in chapter 4.
Read as the portrait of the apostle

Paul is shown as the one through whom the mystery was revealed, the prisoner, the servant and the least of the saints. This is a personal and an official picture at once. Scholars who think the letter was written by a follower of Paul read it as the follower's tribute; others read it as Paul's own account of his calling.

The chapter closes with a prayer that has no request for anything outside the readers' knowing and being. Its four dimensions and its fullness have inspired mystics and preachers, and the doxology has become a common blessing in worship.

views.H: The setting is Paul in custody, perhaps Rome (Acts 28:16-31), perhaps Caesarea or Ephesus (see the note at 3:1). The readers are Gentile Christians in Asia who might wonder why the apostle to the Gentiles is in chains. Paul says his imprisonment is 'for you' and 'your glory'. For many of them it also meant a loss of the support of a great teacher. The sudden 'if you have indeed heard' (3:2) and the lack of names suggest the readers did not all know him in person. His kneeling (3:14) was the posture of urgent prayer. The reference to the 'family' (3:15) would also recall Roman family-heads, and the title Pater Patriae that Rome gave to Augustus.
views.C: The chapter is at the center of the authorship debate. The self-description 'less than the least' with the claim to special insight into the mystery (3:3-4, 8-9) reads to some like later portrait-painting; the 'holy apostles and prophets' of 3:5 is an odd phrase for Paul to use, who in 1 Corinthians 15:9 calls himself the least of the apostles; and the long sentences (3:2-7 is one sentence of 92 Greek words). Defenders of Paul answer that Paul writes of his unique commission in Galatians 1:11-17 and Romans 15:15-21, that 'holy' apostles is not impossible, and that a prisoner dictating at length might speak this way. There are variants at 3:3 (active or passive), 3:9 (plan or fellowship; 'through Jesus Christ') and 3:14 ('of our Lord Jesus Christ') that explain differences in the KJV.
views.L: The chapter has an unusual shape: an unfinished sentence (3:1), a long digression (3:2-13), a restart (3:14) and a prayer in two parts, with a doxology. The digression itself is a single flow of relative clauses that gradually reveal the mystery: 'the mystery... which... that the Gentiles are...' In the Greek, 3:2-7 is one sentence. The key word in the digression is a group of compounds beginning with 'together': heirs together, members of the body together, sharers together. The prayer is built around four verbs of petition (be strengthened, Christ dwell, be able to grasp, know) and a purpose clause ('so that you may be filled'), and it ends with the highest praise in the letter.
views.J: The question for a Jewish reader is what is meant by a 'mystery' that Gentiles are 'heirs together'. The prophets had spoken of the nations coming to Zion (Isaiah 2:2-4; 49:6; 56:6-8; Zechariah 8:20-23), so the idea that Gentiles would turn to the God of Israel was not new. What is new here is that they come as equals, and as Gentiles, with no need to become Jews (compare Acts 15). 'Mystery' has a Jewish setting in Daniel and Qumran (a secret of God revealed to a chosen interpreter). The phrase 'in other generations it was not made known' sits oddly beside the many prophetic promises, and readers ask whether it means that Israel's prophets did not know or that the church only now saw their meaning; see the note at 3:5. The churches' answers on what this means for Israel are on the card.
views.T: Chapter 3 gave the church two of its richest prayers and a debate about the mystery. Augustine read the four dimensions of 3:18 as the shape of the cross (Letter 55). Some readers hear in 'filled with all the fullness of God' the language of sharing in God's life, and Catholic teaching speaks of divinization (Catechism 460). Dispensationalist theologians read 3:3-6 as the 'mystery' of a church distinct from Israel; covenant theologians (Calvin and the Reformed) read it as the widening of the one people of God; Catholics (Lumen Gentium 9) as the people of God now gathered from all nations.

deep.b:
Paul says what the mystery is in 3:6: 'that the Gentiles are heirs together, members of the body together, and sharers together in the promise in Christ Jesus through the good news.' It is not that the Gentiles will be saved, which the prophets had said. It is that they are fellow heirs, fellow body-members and fellow sharers without any of them becoming Jewish first.

Elsewhere, 'the mystery' means other things: the plan to gather all things in Christ (1:9-10), the great meaning of marriage in Genesis 2:24 seen in Christ and the church (5:32), the good news itself (6:19), Christ among the Gentiles (Colossians 1:27) and the full number of Gentiles and the salvation of all Israel (Romans 11:25-26). These are not rival ideas. Each is a way of describing one hidden purpose of God, the union of all things and all peoples in Christ. In Ephesians 3, the mystery is the part of it that concerns Jews and Gentiles.

The phrase 'not made known in other generations' (3:5) has to be read next to Romans 16:26, where the mystery is made known 'through the writings of the prophets' and in 3:10, where the church makes known God's wisdom. The sense is that the full shape of God's plan stayed hidden until Christ, even though parts of it were seen in advance. For the churches' different answers about whether this makes the church a new people or a widened Israel, see the card below.

deep.h: The prayer of 3:14-19: four requests, one aim
deep.b:
The prayer has a simple shape. Paul asks the Father for four things, each leading to the next. (1) That the readers be strengthened with power through the Spirit in their inner selves. (2) That Christ settle in their hearts through faith. (3) That, rooted and founded in love, they have the strength to grasp, with all the saints, the width and length and height and depth. (4) That they know the love of Christ, which goes beyond knowing. The aim is the last line: 'so that you may be filled up to all the fullness of God.'

Notice the order of persons: the Father is addressed, the Spirit strengthens, Christ dwells, and God's fullness fills. Notice too that the verbs ask for knowing, not for doing. Paul's concern here is with the readers' grasp of a love they already have. Notice finally that the knowing is shared: 'with all the saints'. Nothing in the prayer is private.

echoes: Genesis 12:3; Isaiah 2:2-4; Isaiah 49:6; Isaiah 56:3-8; Zechariah 8:20-23; Job 11:7-9; Daniel 2:18-19; Daniel 2:47; Romans 11:25-26; Romans 15:15-21; Romans 16:25-27; 1 Corinthians 2:6-10; 1 Corinthians 4:1; 1 Corinthians 15:9; Galatians 1:11-17; Galatians 2:7-9; Colossians 1:24-29; Colossians 2:1-3; Philippians 1:12-14; 1 Peter 1:10-12; Acts 9:15; Acts 22:21

settings.by: Paul, as the prisoner of Christ Jesus
settings.to: the Gentile readers ('you Gentiles'), who may have heard of him but did not all know him
settings.when: during his imprisonment, a point at which his readers might wonder whether his chains meant failure
settings.why: to tell the readers that his imprisonment is a part of his service to them, that his task was given by revelation and not by human appointment, and that the secret he carries is theirs. It changes how they hear the letter: what has been said about their inclusion (2:11-22) is not an opinion but the content of the revelation God gave Paul. It may also answer a worry: if 'not lose heart' (3:13) is Paul's request to his readers, some of them were discouraged by his suffering (the note at 3:13 gives the other reading).
settings.readers: Gentile Christians in Asia, hearing that the most famous prisoner of the church is suffering for them, and that the church that includes them is meant to be seen by the powers of the heavenly world.
views: A digression, or the heart of the letter
Some scholars treat 3:2-13 as an aside between two halves of a prayer (3:1 and 3:14). Others treat it as the point at which Paul states his own role in the mystery of 2:11-22.

Defenders of Paul's authorship see a personal reflection on his calling. Those who think a follower wrote the letter see a portrait of Paul as the apostle to the Gentiles that serves the later church.

settings.what: Paul's prayer for strength, love and fullness, and the doxology
settings.to: the same Gentile readers, with all the saints
settings.when: after the digression, as the restart of the prayer begun at 3:1; it closes the first half of the letter
settings.why: to ask for the readers what they need to live out the unity of chapter 2: strength in the inner self, Christ's presence, love as their root, and the knowing of a love bigger than they can know. The doxology turns the request into praise. A letter that goes on in 4:1 to ask for the lives of the readers has just prayed that God do the work in them first.
settings.readers: Believers in a city of powers and fear were told that the power at work in them can do far more than they could ask, and that it works from within.
views: As in 1:15-23, the prayer teaches the readers what to want. Its shape (Father, Spirit, Christ, fullness) is read as Trinitarian by later writers, though Paul gives no doctrine here.
Where the first part of the letter ends
Many take 3:21 as the end of the first main division (chapters 1-3), with 4:1 ('I urge you') as the start of the second; the doxology marks the break.

traditions.q: Is the church the new Israel, a widened Israel, or something distinct from Israel (3:6)?
views: The church is the new people of God, which draws life from the root of Israel; the Jews remain beloved for the sake of their ancestors, and God does not take back his gifts and his call (Lumen Gentium 9; Nostra Aetate 4, which cites Ephesians 2:14-16).

Among the fathers the Orthodox church honors, Justin Martyr calls Christians 'the true spiritual Israel' (Dialogue with Trypho 11), while Chrysostom, in his fifth homily on Ephesians (on 2:11-12), asks whether Paul belittles Israel's privilege and answers that he does not: the Gentiles' benefit is fellowship with Israel, as 'fellow citizens of the saints'.
The one church is the assembly of all believers wherever the gospel is preached and the sacraments are given (Augsburg Confession VII).
There is one covenant of grace and one people of God under both testaments (Calvin, Institutes 2.10-11; Westminster Confession 7 and 25).
Dispensationalists hold that Israel and the church have distinct roles and that the church is a separate program, a 'mystery'.

Wikipedia reports that most Messianic Jews reject supersessionism, the view that the church has replaced Israel, and hold that Israel 'has not forfeited its status as God's chosen people.' It says the Messianic Jewish Alliance of America welcomes non-Jews but views Gentiles and Jews as spiritually distinct.
